en: Netti Paṭiniddesavāra Vibhaṅga 12: The Exposition on the Section of Further Exposition.
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Entry.
Therein, what is the mode of conveying entry? It is:
"And that which is dependent arising."
“Released above, below, and everywhere,
not contemplating ‘I am this’—
thus liberated, he has crossed over the flood.”
“Untrodden before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence.
“Above” refers to the form realm and the formless realm.
“Below” refers to the sense realm.
“Completely liberated in every respect”: this is the liberation of one beyond training (*asekkhā-vimutti*) within the three realms.
These very same factors are the five faculties of one beyond training; this is the entry by way of the faculties (*indriya*).

Those very same five faculties of one beyond training are true knowledge (*vijjā*); with the arising of true knowledge comes the cessation of ignorance (*avijjā-nirodha*); with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-nirodha*).

With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
With the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This is the entry into dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Those same five faculties of one beyond training are comprised within three aggregates:
the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom; this is the entry by way of the aggregates.

Those same five faculties of one beyond training are included among formations; those formations which are without taints and are not constituent parts of existence are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements.
That element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is included within the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana); it is that base which is untainted (anāsava), yet is not the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This is the entry by way of the bases.

"Not contemplating ‘I am this’" is the eradication of the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); that is the liberation of one in training (sekkhāvimutti), and those very things are the five faculties of one in training.

This is the entry by way of the faculties. Those same five faculties of one in training are true knowledge (vijjā); with the arising of true knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance; with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; thus is the entire dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
This is the entry into dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That very same clear knowledge (*vijjā*) is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
This is the entry into the aggregates (*khandha*).

That very same knowledge is included within the formations; those formations that are taintless (*anāsava*) and not part of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), those formations are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*). This is the entry by way of the elements.

That element of mental phenomena is included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*); that base which is taintless and not part of the life-continuum—this is the entry by way of the bases.

Through the liberation of the trainee (*sekkhā*) and the liberation of the one beyond training (*asekkhā*), he who is liberated has crossed over the flood, having never crossed before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Above, below. For one who is dependent there is wavering;
for one who is independent there is no wavering. When there is no wavering, there is tranquility. When there is tranquility, there is no inclination.
When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going. When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and rebirth.
“There is [no self]; with the cessation of rebirth and death, there is neither here nor beyond, nor between the two—this itself is the end of suffering.
Regarding the statement, “For one who relies, there is wavering,” reliance is twofold: reliance on craving (*taṇhā-nissaya*) and reliance on views (*diṭṭhi-nissaya*).
Therein, the volition of one who is impassioned is reliance on craving.
The volition of one who is deluded is this reliance on views.
Volition, however, is formations; with formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises. Thus is the entire dependent origination.
This is the entry into dependent origination.
In this regard, the feeling of one who is lustful is pleasant feeling;
the feeling of one who is deluded is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These two feelings constitute the aggregate of feeling.
This is the entry by way of the aggregates.

Therein, pleasant feeling consists of two faculties: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*); neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
This is the entry by way of the faculties.

Those very same faculties, when included within the formations (*saṅkhāra*), are those formations that are subject to taints (*sāsava*) and constitute the constituent of existence (*bhavaṅga*); those formations are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).

That element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) is included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*); that base which is with taints (*sāsava*) and constitutes the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)—this is the entry by way of the bases (*āyatana*).

"Of one who is independent, there is no wavering": this means either, by way of serenity (*samatha*), being independent of craving (*taṇhā*), or, by way of insight (*vipassanā*), being independent of views (*diṭṭhi*).

That which is insight is true knowledge (*vijjā*); with the arising of true knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance (*avijjā*); with the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*); with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
Thus is the entire dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). This is the entry into dependent origination.
That same insight is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
This is the entry by way of the aggregates.
That same insight consists of two faculties:
the faculty of energy and the faculty of wisdom.
This is the entry by way of the faculties (*indriya*).

That same insight (*vipassanā*), when included within formations (*saṅkhāra*), and those formations which are without taints (*anāsava*) but not part of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
That element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is included within the sphere of phenomena (dhammāyatana); it is that sphere which is free from taints (anāsava), yet is not the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This is the entry by way of the spheres.
Regarding the phrase "when there is tranquility," there are two kinds of tranquility: physical and mental.
That which is bodily pleasure is bodily tranquility;
that which is mental pleasure is mental tranquility.
One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated; being concentrated, one understands things as they truly are.
Understanding things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated;
in liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated. One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
Thus he does not incline toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; through the destruction of lust,

the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, by the destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and giving up of that form by which one might describe the Tathāgata as standing or walking, there is the destruction of form.

The Tathāgata, being liberated, does not admit that "he exists," nor does he admit that "he does not exist," nor does he admit that "he both exists and does not exist," nor does he admit that "he neither exists nor does not exist.
Rather, through the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, he is simply reckoned as "deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, one who has attained Nibbāna."
By whatever feeling...
by whatever perception;
by whatever formations.
By means of whatever consciousness one might designate a Tathāgata as standing or walking,
with the destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and abandonment of that consciousness, he is liberated through the destruction of consciousness; thus,

it does not apply that "the Tathāgata exists," nor does it apply that "he does not exist," nor does it apply that "he both exists and does not exist," nor does it apply that "he neither exists nor does not exist."
Then, indeed, it is reckoned simply as "profound," "immeasurable," "innumerable," and "extinguished" due to the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
"Coming" (*āgati*) here means arrival;
"going" (*gati*) means rebirth after death.
“Neither coming nor going” refers to the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattika-āyatana*).
“Neither here” refers to the six external sense bases (*bāhira-āyatana*).
“Nor in between the two” means that one does not perceive a self among those phenomena that arise from contact.
“This indeed is the end of suffering” refers to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
It is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
Therein, the mundane consists of formations conditioned by ignorance, up to aging and death.
In one who possesses the supramundane virtue, non-remorse arises; he understands: "there is no further state of being here.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "For one who is dependent there is wavering; for one who is independent there is no wavering...
this indeed is the end of suffering."
“Whatever sorrows or lamentations there are,
and whatever various forms of suffering exist in the world—
all these arise dependent upon what is dear.”
These do not exist for one who has no endearments.
Therefore, those for whom there is nothing dear anywhere in the world are happy and free from sorrow.
"Therefore, one who desires sorrowlessness and freedom from dust should not form attachment to anything in the world.
"Whatever sorrows or lamentations there are, and whatever various forms of suffering exist in the world— all these arise dependent upon what is dear."
“This is painful feeling.
“When what is dear is absent, these do not come to be”—
this is pleasant feeling.
Feeling is the aggregate of feeling.
This is the entry by way of the aggregates.

With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death—thus it is for all [the factors].
This is the entry into dependent origination.
Therein, pleasant feeling consists of two faculties:
the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy.
Painful feeling consists of two faculties:
the faculty of pain and the faculty of mental grief.
This is the entry by way of the faculties.

Those very same faculties are included within formations; those formations which are with taints and constitute the life-continuum are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements.
That element of mental phenomena is included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*); that base which is with taints constitutes the life-continuum.
This is the entry by way of the sense bases:
"Therefore, indeed, those are happy and free from sorrow,
for whom there is nothing dear anywhere in the world."
Therefore, one who desires sorrowless and stainless peace should not form endearment toward anything in the world.
This is the abandoning of craving.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; thus all [is ceased].
This is the entry into dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That very abandoning of craving is serenity (*samatha*).
Thus, serenity consists of two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.
This is the entry by way of the faculties.
That same serenity is the aggregate of concentration.
This is the entry by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).

That very same serenity (*samatha*) is included within the formations (*saṅkhāra*); those formations which are without taints (*anāsava*) and are not part of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), those formations are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
That element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is included within the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana); it is that base which is free from taints (anāsava), but is not the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This is the entry by way of the bases.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Whatever sorrows... and so forth.
“If one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them,
he will surely be joyful in mind.”
Having obtained what he desires,
if that person, full of longing and with desire arisen, [still seeks more];
Those sensual pleasures fade away;
like one pierced by an arrow, he suffers.
He who completely avoids sensual pleasures—
Like a snake’s head trodden underfoot,
one who is mindful overcomes the attachment to existence in the world.
In this context, that which is mental elation is *anunaya* (favouring).
When it is said, "He is afflicted as if pierced by an arrow," this is *paṭigha* (repulsion).
Now, both favouring and repulsion belong to the side of craving (*taṇhā*), and the ten material sense-bases (*rūpāyatana*) are the footing for that craving.
This is the entry by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Those same ten material things constitute the body of form (*rūpakāya*), which is associated with name (*nāma*); both together are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises—and so on for everything.
This is the entry by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That very same name-and-form is the five aggregates.
This is the entry by way of the aggregates.
That very same name-and-form is the eighteen elements.
This is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).

Therein, that which is the material body consists of these five physical faculties; that which is the mental body consists of these five non-physical faculties. These are the ten faculties (*indriya*).
This is the entry by way of the faculties.
In that regard,
when it is said: "He who avoids sensual pleasures as one would the head of a snake with his foot..."
“Mindful, one overcomes the attachment to existence in the world.
This is the element of nibbāna with residue remaining; this is the entry into the elements.

That very same element of Nibbāna with residue remaining is true knowledge (*vijjā*); with the arising of true knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance (*avijjā*); with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Thus it is for everything.
This is the entry into dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That very same true knowledge is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
This is the entry by way of the aggregates.
That same clear knowledge consists of two faculties:
the faculty of energy and the faculty of wisdom.
This is the entry by way of the faculties (*indriya*).

That same clear knowledge (*vijjā*) is included within the formations (*saṅkhāra*); those formations that are without taints (*anāsava*) and are not part of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) are comprised within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*).
This is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
That element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is included within the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana); it is that base which is free from taints (anāsava), yet is not the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This is the entry by way of the bases.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “For one who desires sensual pleasures...”
To this extent, through dependence, there come to be the convergence and the penetration of the faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases.
Thus, by way of dependence, the faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases are to be penetrated.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "And that which is dependent origination..."
The Mode of Conveying the Entry is concluded.
